cultivar: Local population varieties and other suitable improved cultivars
processing: Withered, fixed at about 200 to 220°C, cooled, shaped, rested for one to five hours, then baked, and finally heated briefly to lift the aroma. Made in a flat shape and in a strip shape, the latter with an extra step of hand-rubbing to bring out the down.
harvest_season: Usually begins around Qingming, using one bud with one just-opening leaf.
appearance_dry: Flat, straight and even in the flat style, tender green in colour; the strip style shows visible down.
appearance_wet: Even, bright yellow-green leaves and buds.
taste_profile: Fresh and clean with a lasting clear fragrance and a sweet return in the aftertaste.

brewing.notes: Usual advice for a tender flat green: let the water cool, leave the lid off, and shorten the steep if it turns sharp.

vintage_note: Sold as the current spring harvest, as usual for tender Chinese greens, with the earliest picking around Qingming. The makers cold-store the finished tea, so buy recent stock and keep it sealed and cool.
description:
Luocun tea is a green from Luocun in Tiexi town, Tongjiang County, on the southern slopes of the Daba Mountains in northern Sichuan. The protected name covers the whole county, so a tin saying Luocun need not come from the village itself.

It comes in two shapes. The flat style is pressed smooth during repeated firing, a little like Long Jing in looks; the strip style is rubbed between the palms until the down shows. Both get a long rest between shaping and baking, and a short final heating that brings up the aroma.

The cup is a tender bright green, with a clear lasting scent and a sweet finish. Flat greens are easy to scald, so cooler water and an uncovered vessel serve it well.

Look for spring lots, and check whether you are getting flat or strip tea, since they drink differently. The tea is also marketed for selenium and other trace elements; those claims say more about the sales pitch than about what is in the cup.
history:
County tradition holds that Tongjiang's tea was already well regarded in the Song dynasty, though the claim comes from local promotion rather than a text anyone quotes. A number of named teas are listed from the area, among them Tiangang Yinya and Luocun Mingmei.

The modern record is firmer: a silver award at a Thai exhibition in 1993, silver and gold awards at Chinese fairs in 1995, a first prize at the Zhongcha Cup in 2005, and national geographical indication protection on 18 July 2012.
